common_name: Majorette Series Gerbera Daisy (Compact Non-Stretching Bedding Gerbera)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Majorette was bred by Sakata specifically for non-stretching stems and uniform, fast bench timing in pot production.

directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably mild. Majorette produces an unusually heavy first flush of blooms over 3 inches across in seven colors including a red bicolor, held on short, sturdy stems that resist the stretching common in older gerbera seed strains. Its compact, uniform habit and fast crop time make it a favorite for quart-pot and larger container production as well as tidy garden edging. Water at the base rather than overhead to reduce crown rot, deadhead spent blooms to keep flowering through the season, and grow as an annual outside its perennial range.

common_name: Winston Churchill Fuchsia (Double Lavender-and-Pink Hardy Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; named British Fuchsia Society Fuchsia of the Year and holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade. Winston Churchill bears fully double flowers with short, reflexed pink sepals over bluish-lavender petals veined in pink, opening earlier in the season than many hardy fuchsia cultivars on a naturally compact, bushy, well-branched plant. Its tidy proportions and heavy early bloom suit a container or the front of a shaded border better than the larger upright hardy types, and it draws hummingbirds throughout its long summer-to-autumn flowering. It dies back to the ground in colder winters and resprouts from the roots each spring; in the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South give it afternoon shade and consistent moisture, and mulch heavily over winter to protect the crown.

common_name: Alice Hoffman Fuchsia (Dwarf Rose-and-White Hardy Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; one of the smallest hardy fuchsia cultivars and a holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade. Alice Hoffman bears small semi-double flowers with rose-red sepals and tube surrounding a white, rose-veined corolla, set against small, bronze-tinted foliage on gracefully arching branches that stay compact without heavy pruning. Its diminutive scale makes it useful for edging a shaded bed or growing in a smaller container where larger hardy fuchsia cultivars would overwhelm the space, and it flowers heavily from early summer to frost, drawing bees and hummingbirds. It dies back to the ground in colder winters and resprouts reliably from the roots each spring; in the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South give it afternoon shade and consistent moisture, and mulch heavily over winter to protect the crown.

common_name: Mrs W P Wood Fuchsia (Pale Pink-and-White Hardy Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; bred by W. P. Wood in 1949 and a holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade. Mrs W P Wood bears small single flowers in pale pink shading to white, a notably soft, understated color for a hardy fuchsia, held above pale green foliage on a vigorous, upright, bushy plant that grows larger than many other hardy cultivars. Its size and reliable, abundant bloom from early summer into fall make it well suited as a flowering hedge or backdrop shrub in a hardy fuchsia border, and it attracts hummingbirds throughout its long season. It dies back to the ground in colder winters and resprouts vigorously from the roots each spring; in the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South give it afternoon shade and consistent moisture, and mulch heavily over winter to protect the crown.

common_name: Cascade Fuchsia (Historic White-and-Red Trailing Basket Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants after frost danger has passed in rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix in shade to partial shade; registered in 1937 by American breeder John Lagen and still a benchmark trailing basket cultivar.

directions: Grow in a hanging basket or shaded container filled with rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix. Cascade bears single flowers with white sepals and tube surrounding deep pinkish-red petals, a strongly contrasting bicolor carried in abundance on vigorous, well-branched trailing stems that fill out a basket quickly. Introduced in the 1930s, it remains one of the most widely grown heirloom trailing fuchsia cultivars and a standard against which newer white-and-red basket types are compared. It has little cold tolerance and dries out quickly as a basket plant, so in the Gulf South site it in a shaded, breezy spot with frequent watering and bring it under cover well before the first fall frost.
